about.p: This course is extra practice for *English Grammar in Use*. Each unit begins with a short reminder of the rules and then gives you plenty of exercises: choosing the right form, typing it yourself, putting right sentences that contain a mistake, and building sentences word by word.

If a point is new to you, study it first in the Grammar in Use course – every unit here tells you which units to look at. Then come back and practise until the right form comes to you without thinking.

The units are not in order of difficulty, so start with the grammar you find hardest. Do the exercises, read the feedback when you make a mistake, and try the unit again a few days later. The review units mix several points together, just as real English does.
Every unit ends with a short writing task. Use it: writing a few sentences of your own is the best way to make the grammar yours.

L.p: Use the present continuous (*am/is/are + -ing*) for something in progress now or around now, and for a temporary situation. Use the present simple (*do/does*) for habits, routines, permanent situations and things that are generally true.

L.e: I'm cooking, so I can't come to the phone. Ana's staying with her cousin until she finds a flat. I cook most evenings. Ana lives in Porto. Water freezes at 0°C.

L.x: How often *do you go* (not *are you going*) to the gym?
What *do you do* (not *are you doing*)? – I'm a nurse.
The sun *rises* (not *is rising*) in the east.

L.tip: Need the rules? See Grammar in Use units 1–3.

L.p: Some verbs describe states, not actions, and we don't normally use them in the continuous: *like*, *love*, *hate*, *want*, *need*, *prefer*, *know*, *understand*, *believe*, *remember*, *mean*, *belong*, *own*, *seem*, *contain*.

L.e: I don't understand this question. Does this bag belong to you? You seem a bit tired today. This drink contains a lot of sugar.

L.x: I *know* (not *am knowing*) the answer.

L.p: Some of these verbs also have an action meaning, and then the continuous is possible: *I think* (= I believe) but *I'm thinking* (= I'm considering); *she has* a car but *she's having* lunch; *I see* (= I understand) but *I'm seeing* the doctor (= meeting).

L.e: Do you think it'll snow tonight? I'm thinking of moving to Bristol. We're having a barbecue on Saturday. I see what you mean.

L.p: *always* + present continuous means 'too often', and usually shows that the speaker is annoyed.

L.e: He's always leaving wet towels on the bathroom floor! You're always checking your phone when I'm talking to you.

L.x: This coat *belongs* (not *is belonging*) to my sister.
*Do you understand* (not *Are you understanding*) what I mean?

L.p: Use the past simple (*did*) for a finished action or a series of actions in the past. Use the past continuous (*was/were + -ing*) for an action in progress at a particular time; it often gives the background to a shorter action in the past simple.

L.e: I rang Mum, made a cup of tea and sat down. At eight o'clock last night I was ironing. While we were walking home, it started to hail. The children were playing outside when the storm began.

L.x: She *didn't know* (not *wasn't knowing*) the answer.

L.p: *when* + past simple often shows one action after another. *while* or *when* + past continuous shows one action in the middle of another.

L.e: When she saw the price, she put the dress back. While Joe was parking the car, a dog jumped onto the bonnet.

L.x: *Did you see* (not *Did you saw*) the eclipse last night?
While I *was waiting* (not *waited*) for the train, I read the paper.

L.h: A have done or have been doing?

L.p: Use the present perfect continuous (*have been doing*) for an activity that has been going on for a period of time, often with a result we can see now. Use the present perfect simple (*have done*) for a completed action or a result, especially when we say how much or how many.

L.e: Your eyes are red. Have you been crying? I've been painting the fence all morning – look at my hands! I've painted half of it. She's sent three emails since lunch.

L.x: I've *read* (not *been reading*) four books this month.

L.h: B How long or how many?

L.p: Ask *How long have you been …?* about an activity that is still going on. Ask *How many/How much have you …?* about the amount done so far. State verbs such as *know*, *have* (= own), *believe* and *be* are not used in the continuous.

L.e: How long have you been learning Spanish? How many countries have you visited?

L.x: We've *known* (not *been knowing*) each other since primary school.
How long *have you been working* (not *are you working*) here?
I've *cleaned* (not *been cleaning*) all five windows.

L.h: A Up to now or a finished time?

L.p: Use the present perfect (*have done / have been doing*) for a period that continues up to now: *today*, *this week*, *ever*, *never*, *so far*, *since …*. Use the past simple (*did*) for a finished time: *yesterday*, *last year*, *in 2015*, *two days ago*, *when I was a child*.

L.e: I've had two coffees today. I had three yesterday. Have you ever been to Iceland? We went there in 2019. She's been working here since June. Before that she worked in a bank.

L.x: I *saw* (not *have seen*) Emma yesterday.

L.p: Use the past simple to ask *When …?* or *What time …?*, because the answer is a finished time.

L.e: When did you arrive? What time did the match start?

L.x: *When did you get* (not *When have you got*) your new phone?

L.p: When a situation began earlier and is still going on now, use the present perfect, not a present tense. Compare *I'm staying with friends* (now) with *I've been staying with friends for a fortnight* (how long).

L.e: Kate is ill. She's been ill since Monday. We're married. We've been married for twenty years. How long has your neighbour had that noisy dog?

L.p: Use *for* + a period of time (*for three weeks*, *for ages*) and *since* + the starting point (*since Monday*, *since 2010*, *since I was a child*).

L.e: I've been waiting for twenty minutes. She's worked here since April.

L.x: He's been in hospital *since* (not *for*) Tuesday.

L.p: *It's* (= it has been) + a period + *since* + past simple says how long ago something last happened.

L.e: It's three years since I last saw Ben. It's ages since we had a proper holiday.

L.h: A Now, up to now, or finished?

L.p: Present simple or continuous: now, or in general. Present perfect: a link between the past and now – something that continues up to now, or a past action with a result now. Past simple: something at a time that is over.

L.e: I work in a bakery. I've worked there since 2021. Before that, I had a job at a garden centre. She's in Paris at the moment. She's been there since Friday. She went there for a conference.

L.x: My parents *have been* (not *are*) married for thirty years.

L.p: After *This is the first time …*, *It's the second time …* and so on, use the present perfect.

L.e: It's the first time I've tried Ethiopian food. It's the third time she's rung this morning.

L.x: This is the third time I *have visited* (not *visit*) Prague.

L.p: Use the present perfect with a period that is not finished: *today*, *this week*, *this morning* (if it is still morning), *recently*, *lately*. Use the past simple with a period that is over: *yesterday*, *last month*, *in March*, *this morning* (if it is now afternoon).

L.e: I haven't seen Leo this week. (The week isn't over.) I didn't see Leo last week. Have you been busy lately? I was very busy in March.

L.p: We often give news with the present perfect, then use the past simple for the details: when, where and how it happened.

L.e: Our cat has had kittens! She had them on Sunday night in the laundry basket. Someone has broken into the school. They got in through a window.

L.x: Ali has broken his arm. He *fell* (not *has fallen*) off his skateboard.

L.p: In British English, *just*, *already* and *yet* usually go with the present perfect.

L.e: I've just had lunch. Have you finished yet? She's already gone home.

L.x: The concert *started* (not *has started*) at eight, so we missed the first song.
I *haven't finished* (not *didn't finish*) my essay yet.

L.p: Use the past perfect (*had* + past participle) for something that happened before another past time or event. It makes the order of events clear.

L.e: When we got to the station, the train had already left. I didn't recognise him because he'd shaved off his beard. She'd never flown before, so she was nervous.

L.x: Before the meeting, I *had read* (not *have read*) the whole report.

L.h: B Four past forms side by side

L.p: Past simple: one event after another. Past continuous: in the middle of an activity. Past perfect: earlier than the time we are talking about. Past perfect continuous (*had been doing*): an activity that went on up to that earlier time.

L.e: When the guests arrived, Mum made coffee. (First they came, then she made it.) When the guests arrived, Mum was making coffee. (She was in the middle of it.) When the guests arrived, Mum had made coffee. (It was ready.) Her eyes were red – she'd been crying.

L.x: When I got home, I realised I *had left* (not *have left*) my bag on the bus.
We *had been driving* (not *have been driving*) for hours before we found a hotel.

L.p: Use *used to* + infinitive for things that happened regularly in the past but don't happen now, and for past states that are no longer true. The negative is *didn't use to*, and the question is *Did you use to …?*

L.e: I used to bite my nails, but I stopped. There used to be a sweet shop next to the school. We didn't use to have a car. Did you use to wear glasses?

L.x: *Did you use to* (not *Did you used to*) play the piano?

L.h: B used to or past simple?

L.p: Don't use *used to* for a single action, or to say how many times or how long something happened. Use the past simple.

L.e: We went to Rome last year. I visited my aunt twice in June.

L.x: I *lived* (not *used to live*) in Spain for three years.

L.p: *would* can also describe repeated actions in the past (not states), often when we remember the past.

L.e: Every Sunday my grandad would take us fishing.

L.x: I *used to* (not *use to*) live in Leeds.
We *didn't use to* (not *didn't used to*) have a car.

L.e: If it's sunny tomorrow, we'll have a picnic. If you don't hurry, you'll miss the bus. I'll lend you my bike if you need it.

L.x: If I *see* (not *will see*) Rosie, I'll give her your message.

L.p: Use *if* + past simple and *would* + infinitive for a situation that is imaginary, unlikely or not true now. The past form doesn't mean past time here.

L.e: If I had more time, I'd learn the guitar. (But I don't have time.) What would you do if you lost your job?

L.x: If I *knew* (not *know*) her number, I'd ring her.

L.p: After *if*, we can use *were* instead of *was*, and we usually say *If I were you* to give advice.

L.e: If it were a bit cheaper, I'd buy it. If I were you, I'd take the job.

L.x: What *would* (not *will*) you do if you lost your passport?
If I *were* (not *am*) you, I'd accept the offer.

L.p: With verbs like *say*, *believe*, *think*, *report*, *know* and *expect*, we can use *It is said that …* or *Somebody is said to …*. This is common in news reports.

L.p: *be supposed to* can mean 'people say'. It can also mean 'it is planned or expected'. *You're not supposed to* means that it isn't allowed.

L.p: In informal English, we often use *get* instead of *be* for things that happen to people, often by accident.

L.p: In most questions, the auxiliary verb (*is*, *do*, *have*, *can* …) comes before the subject. In the present simple and past simple, use *do/does/did*.

L.e: Where are you going? Have you finished? What time does the shop close? Why did she leave?

L.x: What *did you buy* (not *you bought*) at the market?

L.p: When *who*, *what* or *which* is the subject of the question, don't use *do/does/did*.

L.e: Who told you? (Somebody told you.) What happened? Which team won? Compare: Who did you tell? (You told somebody.)

L.x: Who *broke* (not *did break*) the window?

L.p: After *Do you know …?*, *Can you tell me …?* and *I wonder …*, use normal word order (subject + verb) and no *do/does/did*. Use *if* or *whether* when there is no question word.

L.e: Do you know where the station is? Can you tell me what time it starts? I wonder if she got my message.

L.x: Do you know *where she lives* (not *where does she live*)?

L.p: In questions, a preposition often goes at the end.

L.e: Who are you waiting for? What are you talking about? Where do you come from?

L.p: In reported questions, use statement word order (subject + verb) and no *do/does/did*. Use *if* or *whether* for yes/no questions.

L.e: 'Where do you work?' → She asked me where I worked. 'Are you hungry?' → He asked if I was hungry. 'Did you enjoy the film?' → They wanted to know whether we had enjoyed the film.

L.p: Use *tell* or *ask* + object + *to* + infinitive for orders and requests, and *not to* for the negative.

L.e: 'Sit down.' → The teacher told us to sit down. 'Please don't shout.' → She asked them not to shout.

L.x: She asked me *to close* (not *that I close*) the window.

L.p: We can also report with *advise*, *remind*, *warn* and *invite* (+ object + *to*), *offer*, *promise*, *refuse* and *agree* (+ *to*), and *suggest* (+ *-ing* or *that*).

L.p: Some verbs can take *-ing* or *to …*, with a different meaning. *remember doing* = remember something you did before; *remember to do* = remember that you need to do something. *stop doing* = not do it any more; *stop to do* = stop so that you can do something.

L.p: *try to do* = attempt something that may be hard or impossible. *try doing* = do something as a test, to find out whether it solves a problem. *need doing* has a passive meaning: it needs to be done.

L.e: I tried to lift the box, but it was too heavy. If you can't sleep, try drinking warm milk. The grass needs cutting.

L.p: After *like*, *love*, *hate* and *prefer*, both *-ing* and *to …* are usually possible. After *would like*, *would love* and *would prefer*, use *to …*.

L.e: I love walking in the rain. / I love to walk in the rain. I'd like to book a table for four.

L.p: After a preposition (*in*, *at*, *of*, *about*, *for*, *without*, *before*, *after*, *instead of* …), a verb takes the *-ing* form.

L.h: A afraid to do or afraid of doing?

L.p: Countable nouns have a singular and a plural (*a chair*, *two chairs*). Uncountable nouns have no plural, and we don't use *a/an* with them: *advice*, *information*, *news*, *furniture*, *luggage*, *weather*, *traffic*, *work*, *bread*, *money*, *music*.

L.h: A First mention or already known?

L.p: Use *a/an* (singular) or *some* (plural and uncountable) when we mention something for the first time, or when it doesn't matter which one. Use *the* when the listener knows which one we mean – because we've mentioned it before, or because there is only one.

L.p: Don't use *the* when you talk about things or people in general (with plural and uncountable nouns). Use *the* when you mean particular ones.

L.p: We say *go to school*, *be in hospital*, *go to bed*, *be at work*, *go to prison* and *go to university* when we think of the purpose. Use *the* when we mean the building.

L.p: Use *some* in positive sentences and in offers and requests; use *any* in negatives and most questions. *no* = not any.

L.e: I've got some ideas. We haven't got any bread. Would you like some tea? There's no milk left.

L.h: B much, many, a lot, few, little

L.p: *much* + uncountable and *many* + plural are usual in questions and negatives; in positive sentences we usually say *a lot of*. *a few* / *a little* = some (a positive idea); *few* / *little* = not many / not much (a negative idea).

L.e: There isn't much time. How many people came? She's got a lot of friends. I've got a few friends here, so I'm happy. Few people understood him.

L.x: We've got *a little* (not *a few*) time before the train leaves.

L.h: C all, both, neither, each, every

L.e: Both my sisters are teachers. Neither of them likes cooking. You can sit at either end. Every room has a balcony. Each child got a present.

L.p: Use *who* or *that* for people, and *which* or *that* for things. When the relative pronoun is the object of the clause, we can leave it out.

L.p: *in* = inside an area or a space (*in the kitchen*, *in London*, *in a queue*). *on* = on a surface or a line (*on the wall*, *on the floor*, *on the coast*, *on the second floor*). *at* = at a point, or a place where something happens (*at the door*, *at the bus stop*, *at work*, *at a party*).

L.p: We say *in a car / taxi*, but *on a bus / train / plane / bike*. We say *by car / bus / train*, but *on foot*.

L.p: Use *to* for movement towards a place and *into* for movement inside. We *arrive in* a town or country and *arrive at* a building or other place. After *go*, *come* and *get*, *home* has no preposition.

L.p: *get over* = recover from an illness or a shock. *get by* = manage with very little (money, a language). *get through* = finish something difficult, or reach someone by phone. *get round to* = finally find time to do something. *get out of* = avoid doing something you should do.

L.e: It took her weeks to get over the flu. I can get by in French, but I'm not fluent. I tried to ring the council, but I couldn't get through. I finally got round to fixing the shelf. He always gets out of doing the washing-up.

L.p: *go on* = continue, or happen. *go off* = ring (an alarm), explode, or become bad (food). *go out* = stop burning or shining. *go up / down* = increase / decrease. *go through* = experience something difficult, or examine carefully. *go with* = look good together.

L.e: What's going on? The milk has gone off. The fire's gone out. Bus fares are going up again. She's been going through a hard time. Does this tie go with my shirt?

L.x: Prices have *gone up* (not *gone on*) a lot this year.
